newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin-backed governor beats banker in poll.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin-backed governor beats banker in poll.

text.p: Leonid Roketsky, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Russia's main oil-producing region of Tyumen, beat his banker rival in a run-off election on Sunday, Russian news agencies said on Monday.
Roketsky got 58.83 percent of the vote and secured himself a seat in the upper chamber of the Russian parliament. The other candidate, banker Sergei Atroshenko, received 32.94 percent.
Turnout was between 25 and 28 percent in the snow-swept Western Siberian region.

Incumbent governors across Russia, directly appointed by President Boris Yeltsin in 1992, have had to seek election in a string of regional polls and communists and nationalists have been their main opponents.

The daily newspaper Izvestia has said Atroshenko's performance -- he took second place in the first round of the vote -- showed clearly how the new rich Russian elite was gaining strength in its struggle for political power and influence in the lucrative oil business in modern-day Russia.
Tyumen is home to one of Russia's biggest oil companies, the Tyumenskaya Neftyanaya Companiya (Tyumen Oil Co) and its main operating unit Nizhnevartovskneftegaz.
Atroshenko is the head of Tyumensky Kredit Bank and a co-founder of the Siberian Insurance Company.
Atroshenko came ahead of four other communist candidates in the first round of the vote, although Izvestia said he had the lowest rating in opinion polls when the campaign started.

During his campaign Atroshenko printed a free newspaper, flew a group of pensioners to to the United Arab Emirates on a chartered plane and ordered a special issue of the popular satirical Kukly (puppets) television programme, featuring himself, other local celebrities and national politicians.
Atroshenko represented a public organisation called Tyumen-2000, and the newspaper suggested that the current poll was just a rehearsal. The next regional poll is due in 2000.
Russia has held 55 regional elections last year, choosing 41 governors and more polls are due this year.
The elections are not only a test of the government's popularity, but they could also shift the balance of power in the upper house of parliament.
The Kremlin and the opposition have both claimed victory after each round of the regional polls.
The Kremlin says the new governors, many of them from the opposition, will have to compromise with the federal government.
Elections were also held in Sunday in the autonomous Caucasus republics of Adygeya and Kabardino-Balkaria, and the incumbent presidents of both regions were reelected.
